saliva pH and salivary protein levels are significantly altered in HIV infection.

In summary, our research is concerned with

the following: 1) the effect of saliva and saliva pH on HIV infection; 2) the effect of CD4 counts on oral candidiasis; 3) the risk of transmission of HIV infection from occupational exposure; and 4) the effect of dental treatment on HIV-infected individuals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HIV infected persons are at increased risk of oral diseases, and that dentists are at increased risk for occupational HIV infection.
dentists and hygienists should be aware that HIV-infected persons are more susceptible to periodontal disease and candidiasis.
the risk of transmission of HIV infection from a dental procedure is very low.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have a lot of information about how HIV infection affects the oral cavity and we have some information about how we can reduce occupational exposures.
HIV is a systemic illness which has oral manifestations, and dentists should be alert to those manifestations.
we need to be more aggressive in our efforts to educate our patients and to provide them with appropriate information.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need to be aware that we may be exposed to HIV through our work.
the dental profession should be more aware of the oral complications of AIDS, especially the oral lesions, and that we should be prepared to treat them in our patients.
HIV infection is a chronic illness and that dental professionals should treat patients as they would patients with any other chronic disease.
